confirmed: Source: the full 44-page locally archived English manuscript, including appendices, was checked. The first page carries the annual-meeting heading and states that the English translation was proofread by the authors; no journal-version or preprint-revision identifier is printed (PDF p. 1; pp. 39-44, appendices).

One laboratory experiment randomly assigned 169 university students to human-human (HH) or human-AI (HAI) collaboration; lab_rct, individual assignment, between-group structure, and context_class none are supported (PDF p. 1, Abstract; p. 8, Section 2.1; pp. 9-10, Sections 2.2-2.3).
Assigned counts are 55 HAI humans and 114 HH humans, forming 55 HAI dyads and 57 HH dyads. The latter dyad counts must not be treated as counts of people (PDF p. 8, Section 2.1; p. 15, Table 1).

Valid analyzed samples are 155 people for AUT and 164 for PIT, both above the 50-person threshold. The paper reports 14 AUT exclusions and 5 PIT exclusions, with valid data retained separately for each task; no unique total analyzed across either task is stated, supporting the null combined n_analyzed fields and the task-specific counts in prose (PDF pp. 8-9, Section 2.1).

Analyzed dyad counts are HAI 49 and HH 53 for AUT, and HAI 54 and HH 55 for PIT. The AUT HAI count below 50 does not make the entire study a fewer-than-50-people experiment (PDF p. 17, Table 2; p. 21, Table 4; p. 8, Section 2.1).

The AI partner is identified as GPT?5?mini, accessed through the study chat interface. Participants alternated ideas for unusual rubber-band uses (AUT) and chair improvements (PIT), with humans speaking first in HAI (PDF pp. 9-10, Sections 2.2-2.3).

AUT lasted 10 minutes and PIT 15 minutes, in randomized task order with a 3-minute break; AI ideas were limited to 40 Chinese characters with no explanation (PDF p. 10, Section 2.3; pp. 42-43, Appendix 1).

Novelty and usefulness were rated on generated ideas by two graduate students with creativity-research backgrounds, blinded to condition, using a 7-point scale; participant scores averaged their ideas. Fluency counted valid ideas, and flexibility counted categories, with individual and dyad measures distinguished (PDF p. 13, Section 2.5).

AUT human-only novelty contrast is exactly t(124.63) = 2.58, p = 0.029, d = 0.47, favoring Human in HAI over Human in HH; this is distinct from the dyad comparison in Table 2 (PDF p. 17, Section 3.2.2).

PIT human-only novelty contrast is exactly t(129.37) = 2.42, p = 0.045, d = 0.42, and the human-only fluency contrast is exactly t(109.09) = 4.91, p < 0.001, d = 0.94, both favoring Human in HAI over Human in HH (PDF p. 22, Section 3.3.2).

All three reported strings and both novelty effects in the one-line finding match the human-role comparisons, whose analyses are described as linear mixed-effects models (PDF p. 14, Section 2.6; p. 17, Section 3.2.2; p. 22, Section 3.3.2).

The embedded supplement contains forward-flow plots, PIT immediate-perspective-taking APIM coefficients and standard errors, model-fit statistics, and task/AI prompts, at the locations stated in the form (PDF p. 39, Supplementary Figure 1; p. 40, Supplementary Table 1; pp. 40-41, Supplementary Table 2; pp. 42-44, Appendix 1).
The paper is an original experiment rather than a synthesis, so pooled-study counts and pooled estimates are not applicable (PDF pp. 8-15, Method and Data Analysis; pp. 16-27, Results).

The short-screening brief permits up to three main outcomes and explicitly requires core unclear when assignment is random, at least 50 people are analyzed, and output is scored; these deferred fields are not errors, and this paper should proceed to the two-screener pipeline (codex-jobs/lscreen-c673/brief.md, SHORT-version instructions; PDF pp. 8-10 and 13).
summary: The manuscript reports a laboratory experiment randomly assigning 169 students to human-AI or human-human collaboration, with 155 people analyzed for AUT and 164 for PIT, so it should proceed to the two-screener pipeline. The source description, design, counts, and all three recorded statistical contrasts match the PDF, with no corrections needed under the short-form instructions.
